definition: Linguistic categories include Lexical category, a part of speech such as noun, preposition, etc.
details: Syntactic category, a similar concept which can also include phrasal categories Grammatical category, a grammatical feature such as tense, gender, etc. The definition of linguistic categories is a major concern of linguistic theory, and thus, the definition and naming of categories varies across different theoretical frameworks and grammatical traditions for different languages. The operationalization of linguistic categories in lexicography, computational linguistics, natural language processing, corpus linguistics, and terminology management typically requires resource-, problem- or application-specific definitions of linguistic categories. In Cognitive linguistics it has been argued that linguistic categories have a prototype structure like that of the categories of common words in a language.

explainer.lead: Linguistic categories are the classes linguists and systems use to label words and phrases, such as noun or tense. They matter because taggers, parsers, and lexicons depend on consistent category schemes, yet the schemes differ across theories and languages.

tiers.eli5: Just as a library puts books into sections like fiction or history, language tools sort words into groups like nouns or verbs so the computer knows how each word works.
tiers.practitioner: Engineers use part-of-speech and grammatical category tags as features or outputs in tagging and parsing pipelines. A common pitfall is assuming a category set designed for English transfers cleanly to other languages or to a different theoretical framework.
tiers.paperLevel: Categories include lexical categories (parts of speech such as noun or preposition), syntactic categories (which may also cover phrasal categories), and grammatical categories (features such as tense or gender). Their definition and naming vary across theoretical frameworks and grammatical traditions, so no single universal inventory is assumed.

explainer.example: A tagger labels "book" as a noun in "the book" and as a verb in "they book a room", using lexical category to resolve the ambiguity.
